This avoids induction because it posits an objective, albeit unknown, distance from truth that severe testing approximates without assigning likelihood.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If Popper's own later rejection of verisimilitude as a formalizable concept invalidates the metric used to define 'better'.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the definition of 'severe test' implicitly relies on inductive background knowledge about what constitutes a risky prediction.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the leap from 'survived tests' to 'closer to truth' cannot be made without assuming nature's uniformity.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Popper distinguishes between logical probability (which remains zero or undefined for universal laws) and verisimilitude (content of truth minus content of falsity). A theory that survives severe tests has demonstrated higher empirical content and resilience, suggesting it is closer to the truth. The preference is a rational bet on truth-likeness, justified by the logical structure of the tests themselves, not by an inductive inference that the future will resemble the past.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
